READING

**The numbers in full**

VELLACOTT: GBP 3,050,000 (Suilvenaig) + GBP 240,000 (linkspan) − GBP 610,000 (Brindlemere sale) = GBP 2,680,000 net outlay.
TARNSIDE: GBP 1,420,000 (yard) + GBP 310,000 (charter) = GBP 1,730,000 outlay.

VELLACOTT costs GBP 950,000 more upfront.
VELLACOTT saves GBP 190,000 a year in fuel.
Simple payback on the additional capital: GBP 950,000 ÷ GBP 190,000 = **five years**, i.e. roughly by the end of 2031.

Beyond five years, VELLACOTT is GBP 190,000 a year ahead of TARNSIDE on an ongoing basis — and that saving runs for as long as the vessel is in service, which on a 2017 hull could reasonably be another 25–30 years. TARNSIDE's GBP 950,000 upfront saving is a one-off; the fuel penalty is permanent.

**Hull age and future capital exposure**

The Brindlemere hull was clean in March 2026, which is good news. But re-engining her in 2027 produces a vessel with a 1995 hull and new machinery — a 32-year-old ship by the time she re-enters service. Hull surveys will recur, and steelwork requirements that were absent in 2026 will not stay absent indefinitely. The cost is unquantified, but the direction of travel is clear. The Suilvenaig, built 2017, is nine years old and should face no comparable capital demand for a very long time. The two assets are not equivalent even if their passenger and vehicle capacities are identical. VELLACOTT retires a risk that TARNSIDE simply defers.

**The charter and yard risk**

TARNSIDE replaces twelve weeks of Brindlemere service with a chartered vessel at GBP 310,000. That figure is "agreed in principle," not contracted. Charter markets can move; the vessel agreed on may not be available exactly when needed; a relief vessel crewed by an unfamiliar team introduces its own operational uncertainty. January–March is the low season (five crossings a day), so the revenue impact of any shortfall is at its minimum, but the risk is not zero. VELLACOTT carries no equivalent gap: handover is available 2026-11-20, and the Brindlemere valuation holds until 2027-02-11, giving comfortable time to sequence purchase and sale without a break in service.

**The endorsement and master headcount**

Losing two of nine masters to early retirement is real. Seven masters covering eleven crossings a day through a summer season is tighter than nine, and if further absences coincide with the staggered endorsement courses for the remaining seven, there will be months when the rota has very little slack. This is the most operationally uncomfortable feature of VELLACOTT. However: seven is not an unworkable number for a single-vessel operation of this size, endorsement courses are finite, and you can plan the course schedule around the winter timetable when pressure is lower. The disruption is transitional, not structural.

**The insurance unknown**

The broker has not yet quoted on the Suilvenaig. This is an unresolved gap and it would be imprudent to commit before obtaining that quote. A nine-year-old vessel with a clean recent build record will almost certainly be insurable on reasonable terms, and may attract better terms than a 31-year-old hull. But "almost certainly" is not the same as "has been confirmed," and given the route's year-round licence obligations, insurance terms are not optional information. I note this as a condition, not a reason to abandon VELLACOTT.

**Comparing the two risks**

TARNSIDE's risks are: charter availability and performance for twelve weeks, a permanently higher fuel bill, and a steadily ageing hull with uncosted future demands.
VELLACOTT's risks are: a tighter master rota during a transitional period, and an insurance quote not yet in hand.

The TARNSIDE risks are open-ended and grow with time. The VELLACOTT risks are bounded, manageable, and resolve within one to two seasons.

**Verdict**

Five-year payback on the extra capital, followed by GBP 190,000 a year indefinitely, while simultaneously moving from a 1995 hull to a 2017 hull — VELLACOTT is the stronger course. The right sequencing is: obtain the insurance quote immediately; if terms are acceptable, proceed; stagger the endorsement courses through winter 2026–27 to minimise rota exposure; and secure the linkspan contract in parallel with the vessel purchase.

---

READING
  VELLACOTT's GBP 190,000 annual fuel saving repays the GBP 950,000 additional capital cost within five years, after which the saving accumulates indefinitely — and the transaction simultaneously replaces a 31-year-old hull with a nine-year-old one, eliminating the open-ended future capital risk that re-engining the Brindlemere merely defers. The master-rota thinning and the outstanding insurance quote are real concerns but are bounded and manageable, whereas TARNSIDE's fuel penalty and hull-ageing risk are permanent and grow. On close examination the five-year payback figure is the pivot: it is short enough that the decision is financially clear even before accounting for the hull quality improvement.

CALL
  VELLACOTT

GROUNDS
  The GBP 190,000 annual fuel saving recoups the GBP 950,000 extra capital outlay within five years and then runs indefinitely, while VELLACOTT simultaneously trades a 31-year-old hull for a nine-year-old one, making it superior on both financial return and long-term asset risk compared with a re-engining that reduces neither the fuel bill nor the hull's age.
